verses.index_title: Dhritarashtra's Question
verses.index_summary: The blind king asks Sanjaya what his sons and the sons of Pandu did, gathered at Kurukshetra for battle.
verses.sanskrit_text:
धृतराष्ट्र उवाच।
धर्मक्षेत्रे कुरुक्षेत्रे समवेता युयुत्सवः।
मामकाः पाण्डवाश्चैव किमकुर्वत सञ्जय॥ १.१॥
verses.transliteration:
Dhṛtarāṣṭra uvāca:
Dharma-kṣetre kuru-kṣetre samavetā yuyutsavaḥ,
Māmakāḥ pāṇḍavāś caiva kim akurvata Sañjaya.
verses.hindi_meaning: धृतराष्ट्र ने कहा: हे संजय! धर्मभूमि कुरुक्षेत्र में युद्ध की इच्छा से एकत्र हुए मेरे पुत्रों और पाण्डु के पुत्रों ने क्या किया?
verses.english_meaning: Dhritarashtra said: O Sanjaya, gathered at Kurukshetra, ready for battle, what did my sons and the sons of Pandu do?
verses.context:
Dhritarashtra is the father of the Kauravas. The Pandavas are their cousins, and both sides are preparing to fight a war.

Notice one small detail: Dhritarashtra says "my sons" and "the sons of Pandu", separating the two families even though they belong to the same family.
verses.life_lesson: Attachment can affect how we see things. When we become too attached to our own people, opinions, or interests, we may struggle to see a situation fairly.
verses.spiritual_meaning: The Gita begins by showing us how attachment can influence our understanding of *Dharma* — what is right.
verses.reflection_question: Have you ever supported someone simply because they were close to you, even when you knew they might be wrong?

verses.index_title: Duryodhana Approaches Drona
verses.index_summary: Seeing the Pandava army arranged for battle, Duryodhana goes to his teacher Dronacharya.
verses.sanskrit_text:
सञ्जय उवाच।
दृष्ट्वा तु पाण्डवानीकं व्यूढं दुर्योधनस्तदा।
आचार्यमुपसंगम्य राजा वचनमब्रवीत्॥ १.२॥
verses.transliteration:
Sañjaya uvāca:
Dṛṣṭvā tu pāṇḍavānīkaṁ vyūḍhaṁ Duryodhanas tadā,
Ācāryam upasaṁgamya rājā vacanam abravīt.
verses.hindi_meaning: संजय ने कहा: उस समय पाण्डवों की सेना को व्यूह-रचना में खड़ी देखकर राजा दुर्योधन अपने आचार्य (द्रोणाचार्य) के पास गया और उनसे यह वचन बोला।
verses.english_meaning: Sanjaya said: Seeing the Pandava army arranged for battle, King Duryodhana approached his teacher, Dronacharya, and spoke to him.
verses.context:
Duryodhana sees that the opposing army is prepared for war. He then approaches Dronacharya, his teacher in warfare, and begins speaking to him.

The battle hasn't started yet, but Duryodhana's reaction tells us something about what is happening in his mind.
verses.life_lesson:
Sometimes, even when we appear confident, seeing the strength of others can make us feel uncertain.

Remember: what someone shows on the outside doesn't always reflect what they feel inside.
verses.spiritual_meaning: The Gita invites us to look beyond outward appearances. A person's real struggle may be happening within their own mind, long before any external battle begins.
verses.reflection_question: Have you ever felt confident about something until you saw someone else who seemed better prepared than you?

verses.index_title: The Army Arranged by Drona's Student
verses.index_summary: Duryodhana points to the Pandava army, arranged by the son of Drupada, Drona's own student.
verses.sanskrit_text:
पश्यैतां पाण्डुपुत्राणामाचार्य महतीं चमूम्।
व्यूढां द्रुपदपुत्रेण तव शिष्येण धीमता॥ १.३॥
verses.transliteration:
Paśyaitāṁ Pāṇḍu-putrāṇām ācārya mahatīṁ camūm,
Vyūḍhāṁ Drupada-putreṇa tava śiṣyeṇa dhīmatā.
verses.hindi_meaning: हे आचार्य! पाण्डु के पुत्रों की इस विशाल सेना को देखिए, जिसकी व्यूह-रचना आपके बुद्धिमान शिष्य द्रुपदपुत्र (धृष्टद्युम्न) ने की है।
verses.english_meaning: O teacher, look at this mighty army of the sons of Pandu, arranged so skilfully by your intelligent student, the son of Drupada.
verses.context:
Duryodhana points out that the Pandava army has been strategically arranged by Dhrishtadyumna, who was Dronacharya's student.

Notice that Duryodhana specifically reminds his teacher that the person leading this formation was *his own student*.
verses.life_lesson:
Sometimes, insecurity makes us highlight things that trouble us rather than focus on what we need to do.

Duryodhana could simply acknowledge the opposing army, but he draws attention to the fact that his own teacher trained the person helping to lead it.
verses.spiritual_meaning:
When the mind is controlled by fear or rivalry, even our relationships and past experiences can become sources of resentment rather than wisdom.

The lesson is to recognise when our emotions are influencing how we interpret a situation.
verses.reflection_question: Have you ever felt uncomfortable seeing someone succeed because you believed you should be doing better than them?

verses.index_title: Warriors Equal to Bhima and Arjuna
verses.index_summary: Duryodhana begins naming the great archers of the Pandava side: Yuyudhana, Virata and Drupada.
verses.sanskrit_text:
अत्र शूरा महेष्वासा भीमार्जुनसमा युधि।
युयुधानो विराटश्च द्रुपदश्च महारथः॥ १.४॥
verses.transliteration:
Atra śūrā maheṣvāsā Bhīmārjuna-samā yudhi,
Yuyudhāno Virāṭaś ca Drupadaś ca mahā-rathaḥ.
verses.hindi_meaning: इस सेना में बड़े-बड़े धनुर्धर शूरवीर हैं, जो युद्ध में भीम और अर्जुन के समान हैं — जैसे युयुधान (सात्यकि), राजा विराट और महारथी द्रुपद।
verses.english_meaning: Here are mighty warriors, skilled with their bows and as formidable in battle as Bhima and Arjuna — including Yuyudhana, Virata, and the great warrior Drupada.
verses.context: Duryodhana begins listing the powerful warriors standing with the Pandavas. He recognises that their army contains experienced fighters who can pose a serious challenge.
verses.life_lesson:
Acknowledging someone else's strength is important, but how we respond to it matters even more.

If we focus only on how strong others are, we may become overwhelmed before we even begin. Recognising their abilities should help us prepare, not paralyse us with fear.
verses.spiritual_meaning: The mind often magnifies external challenges when it feels threatened. Spiritual awareness helps us recognise reality without allowing fear to control our response.
verses.reflection_question: When you face strong competition, do you focus more on how capable others are or on improving your own abilities?

verses.index_title: More Heroes of the Pandava Army
verses.index_summary: Dhrishtaketu, Chekitana, the King of Kashi, Purujit, Kuntibhoja and Shaibya are named.
verses.sanskrit_text:
धृष्टकेतुश्चेकितानः काशिराजश्च वीर्यवान्।
पुरुजित्कुन्तिभोजश्च शैब्यश्च नरपुङ्गवः॥ १.५॥
verses.transliteration:
Dhṛṣṭaketuś Cekitānaḥ Kāśirājaś ca vīryavān,
Purujit Kuntibhojaś ca Śaibyaś ca nara-puṅgavaḥ.
verses.hindi_meaning: धृष्टकेतु, चेकितान, बलवान काशिराज, पुरुजित्, कुन्तिभोज और मनुष्यों में श्रेष्ठ शैब्य भी (इस सेना में) हैं।
verses.english_meaning: Among them are Dhrishtaketu, Chekitana, the powerful King of Kashi, Purujit, Kuntibhoja, and Shaibya, the finest among men.
verses.context: Duryodhana is naming more of the experienced and powerful warriors supporting the Pandavas. He is emphasising that their army has many capable fighters, not just Bhima and Arjuna.
verses.life_lesson:
Sometimes, a challenge feels bigger when we keep counting everything working against us.

Recognising the difficulties is sensible, but repeatedly focusing on them can increase our anxiety without helping us solve anything.
verses.spiritual_meaning: The mind can become absorbed in the external world — comparing strengths, counting disadvantages, and anticipating threats. Spiritual growth involves learning to observe these thoughts without letting them dominate us.
verses.reflection_question: When you have a difficult task ahead, does listing everything that could go wrong help you prepare — or does it sometimes make you more anxious?

verses.index_title: Great Warriors, Young and Old
verses.index_summary: Yudhamanyu, Uttamauja, Abhimanyu and the sons of Draupadi complete Duryodhana's list.
verses.sanskrit_text:
युधामन्युश्च विक्रान्त उत्तमौजाश्च वीर्यवान्।
सौभद्रो द्रौपदेयाश्च सर्व एव महारथाः॥ १.६॥
verses.transliteration:
Yudhāmanyuś ca vikrānta Uttamaujāś ca vīryavān,
Saubhadro draupadeyāś ca sarva eva mahā-rathāḥ.
verses.hindi_meaning: पराक्रमी युधामन्यु, बलवान उत्तमौजा, सुभद्रापुत्र (अभिमन्यु) और द्रौपदी के पुत्र भी यहाँ हैं — ये सभी महारथी हैं।
verses.english_meaning: Also present are the brave Yudhamanyu, the powerful Uttamauja, Abhimanyu (Subhadra's son), and the sons of Draupadi. All of them are great warriors.
verses.context: Duryodhana finishes listing several of the Pandavas' important fighters. He emphasises that even the younger warriors, including Abhimanyu, are formidable.
verses.life_lesson: Never underestimate someone because they're young or inexperienced compared with you. A person's ability is not determined by age alone.
verses.spiritual_meaning: The Gita encourages us to look beyond superficial judgments. True capability comes from qualities such as courage, discipline, and determination—not merely status or seniority.
verses.reflection_question: Have you ever underestimated someone and later discovered they were far more capable than you expected?

verses.index_title: Duryodhana Turns to His Own Army
verses.index_summary: Duryodhana tells Drona that he will now name the leaders of their own army.
verses.sanskrit_text:
अस्माकं तु विशिष्टा ये तान्निबोध द्विजोत्तम।
नायका मम सैन्यस्य संज्ञार्थं तान्ब्रवीमि ते॥ १.७॥
verses.transliteration:
Asmākaṁ tu viśiṣṭā ye tān nibodha dvijottama,
Nāyakā mama sainyasya saṁjñārthaṁ tān bravīmi te.
verses.hindi_meaning: हे द्विजोत्तम (ब्राह्मणों में श्रेष्ठ)! हमारे पक्ष में भी जो विशिष्ट योद्धा हैं, उन्हें भी जान लीजिए। आपकी जानकारी के लिए मैं अपनी सेना के उन नायकों के नाम बताता हूँ।
verses.english_meaning: O best among Brahmanas, let me now tell you about the distinguished warriors on our side, the leaders of my army, so that you may know them.
verses.context:
Until now, Duryodhana has been describing the strength of the Pandava army.

Now he shifts his attention towards his own army and begins listing its important warriors.
verses.life_lesson:
There is a difference between recognising a challenge and becoming distracted by it.

Duryodhana has spent several verses discussing the opposing army. Now he reminds himself and his teacher of the strengths they possess.

Sometimes, instead of constantly worrying about what others have, we should recognise the strengths and resources available to us.
verses.spiritual_meaning:
Our attention shapes our state of mind. If we constantly focus on what others possess, we may overlook what we already have.

Learning to recognise our own strengths is also a part of self-awareness.
verses.reflection_question: Do you sometimes spend more time comparing yourself with others than recognising how far you've come?

verses.index_title: The Leaders of the Kaurava Army
verses.index_summary: Drona, Bhishma, Karna, Kripa, Ashwatthama, Vikarna and Bhurishrava are named.
verses.sanskrit_text:
भवान्भीष्मश्च कर्णश्च कृपश्च समितिञ्जयः।
अश्वत्थामा विकर्णश्च सौमदत्तिस्तथैव च॥ १.८॥
verses.transliteration:
Bhavān Bhīṣmaś ca Karṇaś ca Kṛpaś ca samitiñjayaḥ,
Aśvatthāmā Vikarṇaś ca Saumadattis tathaiva ca.
verses.hindi_meaning: आप (द्रोणाचार्य), भीष्म, कर्ण, युद्ध में विजय पाने वाले कृपाचार्य, अश्वत्थामा, विकर्ण और सोमदत्त के पुत्र (भूरिश्रवा) भी (हमारी सेना में) हैं।
verses.english_meaning: Yourself (Dronacharya), Bhishma, Karna, Kripacharya, Ashwatthama, Vikarna, and the son of Somadatta (Bhurishrava) are among our great warriors.
verses.context:
Duryodhana begins naming the strongest warriors on his own side.

He mentions experienced fighters, including Bhishma and Dronacharya, as well as Karna and others.

He is reminding everyone that their army also has powerful and experienced warriors.
verses.life_lesson:
Having capable people around you is a strength, but you should never take that strength for granted.

Whether in work, relationships, or personal life, having good people beside you matters. But you must also learn to recognise and value their contributions.
verses.spiritual_meaning:
The Gita encourages us to recognise the support and resources available to us rather than becoming consumed by comparison.

However, remember that having strength around you doesn't automatically mean your decisions are right. Wisdom is just as important as strength.
verses.reflection_question: Do you genuinely appreciate the people who support you, or do you sometimes realize their importance only when you need them?

verses.index_title: Many Ready to Die for Duryodhana
verses.index_summary: Many other skilled warriors, Duryodhana says, are prepared to give their lives for him.
verses.sanskrit_text:
अन्ये च बहवः शूरा मदर्थे त्यक्तजीविताः।
नानाशस्त्रप्रहरणाः सर्वे युद्धविशारदाः॥ १.९॥
verses.transliteration:
Anye ca bahavaḥ śūrā madarthe tyakta-jīvitāḥ,
Nānā-śastra-praharaṇāḥ sarve yuddha-viśāradāḥ.
verses.hindi_meaning: मेरे लिए अपने जीवन का मोह त्याग देने वाले और भी बहुत-से शूरवीर हैं। वे सभी अनेक प्रकार के शस्त्रों से सुसज्जित हैं और युद्ध-कला में निपुण हैं।
verses.english_meaning: There are many other brave warriors who are prepared to sacrifice their lives for my sake. They are equipped with different weapons and are all highly skilled in warfare.
verses.context:
Duryodhana has finished naming several important warriors. Now he emphasises that many other capable fighters are also standing with him.

He believes he has a powerful army whose warriors are willing to fight and even die for him.
verses.life_lesson:
Having people who stand beside you during difficult situations is valuable.

But there's something important to remember: having people's loyalty doesn't necessarily mean you're making the right decisions.

A good leader doesn't just expect loyalty; a good leader also takes responsibility for the people who trust them.
verses.spiritual_meaning:
The Gita reminds us that external strength and support are not the same as inner wisdom.

You may have resources, loyal people, and great abilities, but without the right understanding of *Dharma*, those strengths can be directed towards the wrong purpose.
verses.reflection_question: If someone is extremely loyal to you and supports you in everything, would you prefer that person to always agree with you, or would you want them to disagree whenever they genuinely believe you're making a mistake?

verses.index_title: Two Armies Compared
verses.index_summary: Duryodhana compares his army, protected by Bhishma, with the Pandava army, protected by Bhima.
verses.sanskrit_text:
अपर्याप्तं तदस्माकं बलं भीष्माभिरक्षितम्।
पर्याप्तं त्विदमेतेषां बलं भीमाभिरक्षितम्॥ १.१०॥
verses.transliteration:
Aparyāptaṁ tad asmākaṁ balaṁ Bhīṣmābhirakṣitam,
Paryāptaṁ tv idam eteṣāṁ balaṁ Bhīmābhirakṣitam.
verses.hindi_meaning: भीष्म द्वारा रक्षित हमारी वह सेना अपार (असीमित) है, जबकि भीम द्वारा रक्षित इन (पाण्डवों) की यह सेना सीमित है।
verses.hindi_meaning_note: The words *aparyāptam* and *paryāptam* can be read in two ways. This translation follows the reading "unlimited" and "limited", as in the English meaning. They can also mean "insufficient" and "sufficient", which would make the verse an admission of Duryodhana's hidden anxiety about his own army. Commentators differ on which sense is intended.
verses.english_meaning: Our army, protected by Bhishma, is unlimited, whereas the army of the Pandavas, protected by Bhima, is limited.
verses.context:
Duryodhana compares the strength of both armies.

He expresses confidence in his own army because Bhishma, a great warrior, is protecting it.

However, there are different interpretations of the Sanskrit words *aparyāptam* and *paryāptam*. They can also convey the sense of insufficient and sufficient. The verse is therefore sometimes understood as revealing Duryodhana's hidden insecurity despite his outward confidence.
verses.life_lesson:
Confidence and insecurity can exist inside the same person.

Sometimes we convince ourselves that we are stronger or better prepared because we need reassurance, not necessarily because we have objectively assessed the situation.
verses.spiritual_meaning:
The Gita encourages us to distinguish between genuine confidence and the ego's need to feel superior.

True inner strength doesn't require constantly proving that we are stronger than someone else.
verses.reflection_question: When you feel confident about something, do you usually trust your own abilities, or do you sometimes need reassurance from others that you're capable?

verses.index_title: Everyone Must Protect Bhishma
verses.index_summary: Duryodhana orders all his warriors to hold their positions and guard Bhishma.
verses.sanskrit_text:
अयनेषु च सर्वेषु यथाभागमवस्थिताः।
भीष्ममेवाभिरक्षन्तु भवन्तः सर्व एव हि॥ १.११॥
verses.transliteration:
Ayaneṣu ca sarveṣu yathā-bhāgam avasthitāḥ,
Bhīṣmam evābhirakṣantu bhavantaḥ sarva eva hi.
verses.hindi_meaning: इसलिए सेना के सभी मोर्चों पर अपने-अपने स्थान पर स्थित रहते हुए आप सब लोग निश्चय ही भीष्म पितामह की ही सब ओर से रक्षा करें।
verses.english_meaning: Therefore, all of you, positioned at your respective places in the different divisions of the army, must protect Bhishma from every side.
verses.context:
After describing the strength of his army, Duryodhana gives an instruction: everyone must protect Bhishma, their commander-in-chief.

Notice something interesting: despite having such a powerful army, he specifically emphasises protecting one person.
verses.life_lesson:
Even the strongest people need support.

Being capable doesn't mean you never need anyone. Sometimes, the people everyone depends on also need someone to stand beside them.
verses.spiritual_meaning:
Strength and dependence are not opposites.

The Gita encourages us to understand that no individual exists entirely independently. We all have relationships, responsibilities and support systems.
verses.reflection_question: Do you find it easy to ask someone for help when you need it, or is your first instinct to handle everything yourself?

verses.index_title: Bhishma Sounds His Conch
verses.index_summary: To cheer Duryodhana, Bhishma roars like a lion and blows his conch.
verses.sanskrit_text:
तस्य सञ्जनयन्हर्षं कुरुवृद्धः पितामहः।
सिंहनादं विनद्योच्चैः शङ्खं दध्मौ प्रतापवान्॥ १.१२॥
verses.transliteration:
Tasya sañjanayan harṣaṁ Kuru-vṛddhaḥ pitāmahaḥ,
Siṁha-nādaṁ vinadyoccaiḥ śaṅkhaṁ dadhmau pratāpavān.
verses.hindi_meaning: उस समय कुरुवंश के वृद्ध, प्रतापी पितामह भीष्म ने दुर्योधन के हृदय में हर्ष उत्पन्न करते हुए ऊँचे स्वर में सिंह के समान गर्जना करके अपना शंख बजाया।
verses.english_meaning: Then the mighty grandsire Bhishma, the oldest and most respected member of the Kuru family, blew his conch loudly like a lion's roar, bringing joy to Duryodhana.
verses.context:
Bhishma notices Duryodhana's state of mind and blows his conch to encourage him and boost the morale of the Kaurava army.

The sound of the conch signals the beginning of the great battle.
verses.life_lesson:
Sometimes, a little encouragement from someone we respect can make a significant difference to our mindset.

But remember, encouragement gives us strength; it doesn't necessarily make our decisions right.
verses.spiritual_meaning: Bhishma's action reminds us that external encouragement can strengthen our minds. However, true wisdom requires more than courage or motivation. It requires knowing whether we're standing on the side of *Dharma*.
verses.reflection_question: When you're feeling uncertain or low, does encouragement from someone you respect genuinely change your mindset, or do you prefer to motivate yourself?

verses.index_title: The Kaurava Army Responds
verses.index_summary: Conches, drums and horns sound together, filling the field with a tremendous noise.
verses.sanskrit_text:
ततः शङ्खाश्च भेर्यश्च पणवानकगोमुखाः।
सहसैवाभ्यहन्यन्त स शब्दस्तुमुलोऽभवत्॥ १.१३॥
verses.transliteration:
Tataḥ śaṅkhāś ca bheryaś ca paṇavānaka-gomukhāḥ,
Sahasaivābhyahanyanta sa śabdas tumulo 'bhavat.
verses.hindi_meaning: इसके बाद शंख, भेरी (नगाड़े), पणव, आनक (ढोल जैसे वाद्य) और गोमुख (नरसिंघे) एक साथ अचानक बज उठे। उनका वह सम्मिलित स्वर अत्यंत भयंकर था।
verses.english_meaning: After that, conches, drums, trumpets and other musical instruments were suddenly sounded together, creating a tremendous noise.
verses.context:
After Bhishma blows his conch, the entire Kaurava army responds with its instruments.

The battlefield fills with a powerful sound, signalling that the war is about to begin.
verses.life_lesson:
When many people come together for a common purpose, their combined energy can be incredibly powerful.

But remember, a large group moving in the same direction doesn't automatically mean they're moving in the right direction.
verses.spiritual_meaning:
The loud sounds represent the external world, full of activity, excitement and pressure.

Sometimes, we become so surrounded by external noise that we forget to listen to our own conscience.

Learning to maintain inner clarity amid external noise is an important part of spiritual growth.
verses.reflection_question: When everyone around you is excited, worried, or convinced about something, do you tend to get influenced by their emotions, or can you maintain your own perspective?

verses.index_title: Krishna and Arjuna Sound Their Conches
verses.index_summary: Seated in their great chariot drawn by white horses, Krishna and Arjuna blow their divine conches.
verses.sanskrit_text:
ततः श्वेतैर्हयैर्युक्ते महति स्यन्दने स्थितौ।
माधवः पाण्डवश्चैव दिव्यौ शङ्खौ प्रदध्मतुः॥ १.१४॥
verses.transliteration:
Tataḥ śvetair hayair yukte mahati syandane sthitau,
Mādhavaḥ Pāṇḍavaś caiva divyau śaṅkhau pradadhmatuḥ.
verses.hindi_meaning: इसके बाद श्वेत घोड़ों से जुते हुए विशाल रथ पर बैठे माधव (श्रीकृष्ण) और पाण्डुपुत्र अर्जुन ने भी अपने दिव्य शंख बजाए।
verses.english_meaning: Then Madhava (Lord Krishna) and Arjuna, seated in their magnificent chariot drawn by white horses, blew their divine conches.
verses.context:
Until now, we've heard about the Kaurava army preparing for battle.

Now the attention shifts to Krishna and Arjuna.

Krishna is Arjuna's charioteer, and both blow their conches in response to the Kaurava army.

This marks the beginning of the Pandavas' response.
verses.life_lesson:
Sometimes, you don't need to react immediately to what others are doing.

You can observe the situation, understand what's happening, and respond at the right moment.
verses.spiritual_meaning:
Krishna is not merely Arjuna's charioteer in this story. He represents divine guidance.

One beautiful way to understand this is: when we allow wisdom to guide our actions, we are less likely to be controlled by external pressure.
verses.reflection_question: When someone challenges you or questions your abilities, is your first instinct to prove yourself immediately, or do you prefer to stay calm and respond through your actions?

verses.index_title: The Conches of Krishna, Arjuna and Bhima
verses.index_summary: Krishna blows Panchajanya, Arjuna blows Devadatta and Bhima blows the great conch Paundra.
verses.sanskrit_text:
पाञ्चजन्यं हृषीकेशो देवदत्तं धनञ्जयः।
पौण्ड्रं दध्मौ महाशङ्खं भीमकर्मा वृकोदरः॥ १.१५॥
verses.transliteration:
Pāñcajanyaṁ Hṛṣīkeśo Devadattaṁ Dhanañjayaḥ,
Pauṇḍraṁ dadhmau mahā-śaṅkhaṁ bhīma-karmā Vṛkodaraḥ.
verses.hindi_meaning: हृषीकेश (श्रीकृष्ण) ने पाञ्चजन्य नामक शंख, धनंजय (अर्जुन) ने देवदत्त नामक शंख और भयानक कर्म करने वाले वृकोदर (भीम) ने पौण्ड्र नामक महाशंख बजाया।
verses.english_meaning: Krishna (Hrishikesha) blew his conch named Panchajanya, Arjuna (Dhananjaya) blew Devadatta, and Bhima (Vrikodara), known for his mighty deeds, blew his great conch named Paundra.
verses.context: The Pandava side now begins responding to the Kauravas' declaration. Notice that the verse identifies each warrior and his individual conch. They are united, but each has a distinct identity and role.
verses.life_lesson:
A team doesn't become strong because everyone is the same. It becomes strong when people with different abilities contribute towards a shared purpose.

Sometimes your strength may be planning, someone else's may be taking action, and another person's may be keeping everyone steady.
verses.spiritual_meaning: Krishna's presence among the Pandavas is significant. Beyond the sound of the conches, the verse reminds us that action gains deeper direction when guided by wisdom.
verses.reflection_question: When you're part of a team, do you naturally prefer taking responsibility for a task yourself, or are you comfortable trusting others to handle their own responsibilities—even when they approach things differently from you?

verses.index_title: Yudhishthira, Nakula and Sahadeva Join In
verses.index_summary: Yudhishthira blows Anantavijaya; Nakula and Sahadeva blow Sughosha and Manipushpaka.
verses.sanskrit_text:
अनन्तविजयं राजा कुन्तीपुत्रो युधिष्ठिरः।
नकुलः सहदेवश्च सुघोषमणिपुष्पकौ॥ १.१६॥
verses.transliteration:
Ananta-vijayaṁ rājā Kuntī-putro Yudhiṣṭhiraḥ,
Nakulaḥ Sahadevaś ca Sughoṣa-Maṇipuṣpakau.
verses.hindi_meaning: कुन्तीपुत्र राजा युधिष्ठिर ने अनन्तविजय नामक शंख बजाया, तथा नकुल और सहदेव ने क्रमशः सुघोष और मणिपुष्पक नामक शंख बजाए।
verses.english_meaning: King Yudhishthira, the son of Kunti, blew his conch named Anantavijaya. Nakula and Sahadeva blew their conches named Sughosha and Manipushpaka.
verses.context: The other Pandava brothers now join Krishna, Arjuna, and Bhima in sounding their conches. The entire Pandava side is making its presence known.
verses.life_lesson:
Not every contribution needs to be the loudest or most noticeable to matter.

Yudhishthira, Nakula, and Sahadeva may not receive the same attention as Arjuna or Bhima in this moment, but they are equally part of the collective effort.

In life, don't measure your importance only by how much attention your contribution receives.
verses.spiritual_meaning: The five Pandava brothers represent different qualities and responsibilities, yet they stand together. Spiritually, this can remind us that different strengths can work in harmony when guided by a shared sense of purpose.
verses.reflection_question: When your contribution goes unnoticed, does it bother you, or are you generally satisfied as long as you know you've done your part properly?

verses.index_title: The Allies of the Pandavas
verses.index_summary: The King of Kashi, Shikhandi, Dhrishtadyumna, Virata and Satyaki stand with the Pandavas.
verses.sanskrit_text:
काश्यश्च परमेष्वासः शिखण्डी च महारथः।
धृष्टद्युम्नो विराटश्च सात्यकिश्चापराजितः॥ १.१७॥
verses.transliteration:
Kāśyaś ca parameṣvāsaḥ Śikhaṇḍī ca mahā-rathaḥ,
Dhṛṣṭadyumno Virāṭaś ca Sātyakiś cāparājitaḥ.
verses.hindi_meaning: श्रेष्ठ धनुर्धर काशिराज, महारथी शिखण्डी, धृष्टद्युम्न, राजा विराट और कभी पराजित न होने वाले सात्यकि ने भी (अपने-अपने शंख बजाए)।
verses.english_meaning: The great archer King of Kashi, the mighty warrior Shikhandi, Dhrishtadyumna, King Virata, and the undefeated Satyaki were also present among the Pandava warriors.
verses.context: The verse continues listing the important warriors on the Pandava side. It reminds us that their army consists of many capable individuals, not just the five Pandava brothers and Krishna.
verses.life_lesson:
We often recognise only the most visible people in a group and overlook the contributions of others.

But a successful team is rarely built by just its most famous or powerful members. There are people whose abilities may not be immediately visible but are still essential.
verses.spiritual_meaning: The verse shows the diversity of people standing together for a common cause. Spiritually, it can remind us that everyone has a different role to fulfil, and no single individual represents the entirety of a greater purpose.
verses.reflection_question: When you meet someone who is less experienced or less recognised than you, do you naturally give them a chance to prove their abilities, or do you initially judge them based on what you see?

verses.index_title: The Next Generation Sounds Its Conches
verses.index_summary: Drupada, the sons of Draupadi and Abhimanyu each blow their own conches.
verses.sanskrit_text:
द्रुपदो द्रौपदेयाश्च सर्वशः पृथिवीपते।
सौभद्रश्च महाबाहुः शङ्खान्दध्मुः पृथक्पृथक्॥ १.१८॥
verses.transliteration:
Drupado draupadeyāś ca sarvaśaḥ pṛthivī-pate,
Saubhadraś ca mahā-bāhuḥ śaṅkhān dadhmuḥ pṛthak pṛthak.
verses.hindi_meaning: हे राजन् (धृतराष्ट्र)! द्रुपद, द्रौपदी के पुत्रों और महाबाहु सुभद्रापुत्र (अभिमन्यु) ने भी सब ओर से अलग-अलग अपने-अपने शंख बजाए।
verses.english_meaning: O King, Drupada, the sons of Draupadi, and the mighty-armed son of Subhadra (Abhimanyu) all blew their respective conches.
verses.context:
Sanjaya continues describing the Pandava warriors sounding their conches. Even more members of their side join in, including the next generation of the family.

The battlefield is now filled with the sound of the Pandavas' conches.
verses.life_lesson:
A strong foundation becomes even stronger when the next generation carries forward the responsibility.

But remember, carrying forward someone's legacy doesn't mean blindly copying them. It means learning from what came before and contributing something of your own.
verses.spiritual_meaning: The verse includes warriors from different generations standing together. It reminds us that duty and purpose can extend beyond one individual or one generation.
verses.reflection_question: When someone has helped you grow or achieve something, do you feel a responsibility to carry forward what they taught you, or do you prefer to build your own path independently?

verses.index_title: A Sound That Shakes the Kauravas
verses.index_summary: The roar of the Pandavas' conches fills sky and earth and pierces the hearts of Dhritarashtra's sons.
verses.sanskrit_text:
स घोषो धार्तराष्ट्राणां हृदयानि व्यदारयत्।
नभश्च पृथिवीं चैव तुमुलोऽभ्यनुनादयन्॥ १.१९॥
verses.transliteration:
Sa ghoṣo dhārtarāṣṭrāṇāṁ hṛdayāni vyadārayat,
Nabhaś ca pṛthivīṁ caiva tumulo 'bhyanunādayan.
verses.hindi_meaning: उस भयंकर घोष ने आकाश और पृथ्वी को गुँजाते हुए धृतराष्ट्र के पुत्रों के हृदय विदीर्ण कर दिए।
verses.english_meaning: The tremendous sound of the Pandavas' conches echoed through the sky and across the earth, piercing the hearts of Dhritarashtra's sons with fear.
verses.context:
Until now, we've heard about the Kauravas sounding their conches, followed by the Pandavas responding. Now Sanjaya describes the impact of that response: the powerful sound unsettles the Kaurava army.

Notice how the atmosphere has changed. What began as a declaration of confidence has become a moment of psychological pressure.
verses.life_lesson:
Sometimes, your preparation and actions speak louder than your words.

You don't always need to announce your abilities or convince others that you're capable. When the moment comes, let your work speak for itself.
verses.spiritual_meaning: The Pandavas' conches can be understood symbolically as the declaration of righteousness and inner conviction. When someone stands firmly behind what they believe is right, that conviction can challenge those who stand on the opposite side.
verses.reflection_question: Have you ever been in a situation where you were underestimated, but instead of arguing or explaining yourself, you let your actions prove what you were capable of?

verses.index_title: Arjuna Raises His Bow
verses.index_summary: Seeing the Kauravas ready for battle, Arjuna lifts his bow as the fighting is about to begin.
verses.sanskrit_text:
अथ व्यवस्थितान्दृष्ट्वा धार्तराष्ट्रान् कपिध्वजः।
प्रवृत्ते शस्त्रसम्पाते धनुरुद्यम्य पाण्डवः॥ १.२०॥
verses.transliteration:
Atha vyavasthitān dṛṣṭvā dhārtarāṣṭrān Kapi-dhvajaḥ,
Pravṛtte śastra-sampāte dhanur udyamya Pāṇḍavaḥ.
verses.hindi_meaning: इसके बाद कपिध्वज (जिनके रथ की ध्वजा पर हनुमान का चिह्न है) पाण्डुपुत्र अर्जुन ने धृतराष्ट्र के पुत्रों को युद्ध के लिए व्यवस्थित खड़ा देखा, और जब शस्त्र चलने ही वाले थे, तब अपना धनुष उठा लिया।
verses.english_meaning: Then, seeing the sons of Dhritarashtra standing ready for battle, Arjuna, whose chariot bore the emblem of Hanuman, lifted his bow as the battle was about to begin.
verses.context:
The conches have sounded. Both armies are positioned, and the moment of battle has arrived.

Arjuna lifts his bow, ready to fight. But what happens next is important: instead of immediately attacking, he asks Krishna to place the chariot between the two armies so he can observe those gathered there.

This request leads to one of the most important turning points in the Bhagavad Gita.
verses.life_lesson:
There is a difference between being ready to act and understanding what you're about to act upon.

Sometimes, just before making an important decision, you need to pause, observe the situation, and understand its consequences.

A pause isn't always hesitation. Sometimes it's preparation for a wiser decision.
verses.spiritual_meaning:
Arjuna represents the human mind facing a difficult choice. Even when we believe we are prepared, deeper reflection can reveal questions we haven't considered.

The Gita begins its central teaching not with an immediate action, but with a moment of observation.
verses.reflection_question: When you're about to make an important decision, do you usually act once you've made up your mind, or do you sometimes pause and reconsider—even when you're already prepared to move forward?

verses.index_title: Place My Chariot Between the Armies
verses.index_summary: Arjuna asks Krishna to place his chariot between the two armies.
verses.sanskrit_text:
अर्जुन उवाच।
सेनयोरुभयोर्मध्ये रथं स्थापय मेऽच्युत॥ १.२१॥
verses.transliteration:
Arjuna uvāca:
Senayor ubhayor madhye rathaṁ sthāpaya me 'cyuta.
verses.hindi_meaning: अर्जुन ने कहा: हे अच्युत (श्रीकृष्ण)! मेरे रथ को दोनों सेनाओं के बीच में खड़ा कीजिए।
verses.english_meaning: Arjuna said: O Achyuta (Krishna), please place my chariot between the two armies.
verses.context:
Arjuna doesn't immediately begin fighting. He asks Krishna to position the chariot between both armies so he can properly observe the people standing there.

Notice something important: Arjuna is not asking to retreat or avoid the battle. He simply wants to see the situation for himself before proceeding.
verses.life_lesson:
Sometimes, before making a difficult decision, you need to step back and look at the situation from a different perspective.

You may have already decided what you're going to do, but understanding the people, circumstances, and consequences can change how you approach it.
verses.spiritual_meaning:
Arjuna asks Krishna to guide his chariot. Symbolically, this can represent the human mind seeking guidance from a higher source of wisdom.

Rather than allowing impulses to control our direction, we can learn to let wisdom guide our actions.
verses.reflection_question: When you face a difficult situation, do you prefer understanding the complete picture yourself, or are you comfortable asking someone you trust to show you a perspective you might be missing?

verses.index_title: Arjuna Wishes to See His Opponents
verses.index_summary: Arjuna wants to look at those eager to fight and see whom he must face in this battle.
verses.sanskrit_text:
यावदेतान्निरीक्षेऽहं योद्धुकामानवस्थितान्।
कैर्मया सह योद्धव्यमस्मिन् रणसमुद्यमे॥
verses.transliteration:
Yāvad etān nirīkṣe 'haṁ yoddhu-kāmān avasthitān,
Kair mayā saha yoddhavyam asmin raṇa-samudyame.
verses.hindi_meaning: (रथ को वहाँ तब तक खड़ा रखिए,) जब तक मैं युद्ध की इच्छा से यहाँ खड़े इन योद्धाओं को भली-भाँति देख न लूँ कि इस युद्ध के उद्यम में मुझे किन-किनके साथ लड़ना है।
verses.english_meaning: Let me observe those who are standing here, eager to fight. I want to see who I will have to fight against in this battle.
verses.context:
Arjuna wants to examine the people assembled on the battlefield.

He isn't satisfied with simply knowing that an opposing army is standing before him. He wants to understand exactly who is involved in the conflict.

This is the beginning of his deeper emotional struggle.
verses.life_lesson:
Sometimes, knowing what you're doing isn't enough. You also need to understand why you're doing it and what you're getting yourself into.

Before committing yourself to something, understand the people involved, the responsibilities you're accepting, and the consequences of your decision.
verses.spiritual_meaning:
Arjuna's request represents the beginning of self-examination.

Before acting, he wants to see the reality in front of him. Spiritually, this reminds us that self-awareness begins when we are willing to look closely at situations rather than simply following our initial assumptions.
verses.reflection_question: When you commit yourself to someone or something you deeply care about, do you sometimes overlook the difficulties or sacrifices involved because your emotions make the decision feel worthwhile?

verses.index_title: Those Who Came to Please Duryodhana
verses.index_summary: Arjuna wants to see the warriors who have gathered to serve the wishes of Duryodhana.
verses.sanskrit_text:
योत्स्यमानानवेक्षेऽहं य एतेऽत्र समागताः।
धार्तराष्ट्रस्य दुर्बुद्धेर्युद्धे प्रियचिकीर्षवः॥ १.२३॥
verses.transliteration:
Yotsyamānān avekṣe 'haṁ ya ete 'tra samāgatāḥ,
Dhārtarāṣṭrasya durbuddher yuddhe priya-cikīrṣavaḥ.
verses.hindi_meaning: दुर्बुद्धि दुर्योधन (धृतराष्ट्र के पुत्र) का युद्ध में प्रिय करने की इच्छा से जो-जो राजा यहाँ एकत्र हुए हैं, उन युद्ध करने वालों को मैं देखना चाहता हूँ।
verses.english_meaning: I wish to observe those who have gathered here to fight, wishing to please the evil-minded son of Dhritarashtra (Duryodhana).
verses.context:
Arjuna wants to see the warriors who have gathered to support Duryodhana.

Notice that he describes Duryodhana as someone of poor judgement and believes these warriors have assembled to support him.

Arjuna is still approaching the battlefield with the mindset that he knows who is right and who is wrong. But soon, seeing the people standing before him will shake that certainty.
verses.life_lesson:
Sometimes, we become so focused on the purpose of a conflict that we forget to consider the personal relationships involved.

You may believe you're fighting for the right reason, but the situation can become much harder when people you know, respect, or love are on the opposite side.
verses.spiritual_meaning:
This verse introduces an important conflict between intellectual judgement and emotional attachment.

Arjuna believes he understands the righteousness of the war, but understanding something intellectually and accepting its emotional consequences are two different things.
verses.reflection_question: Have you ever strongly believed that you were right about a situation, but when you discovered who would be affected by your decision, you started questioning whether you could actually go through with it?

verses.index_title: Krishna Places the Chariot
verses.index_summary: As Arjuna asked, Krishna places the finest of chariots between the two armies.
verses.sanskrit_text:
सञ्जय उवाच।
एवमुक्तो हृषीकेशो गुडाकेशेन भारत।
सेनयोरुभयोर्मध्ये स्थापयित्वा रथोत्तमम्॥ १.२४॥
verses.transliteration:
Sañjaya uvāca:
Evam ukto Hṛṣīkeśo Guḍākeśena Bhārata,
Senayor ubhayor madhye sthāpayitvā rathottamam.
verses.hindi_meaning: संजय ने कहा: हे भारत (धृतराष्ट्र)! गुडाकेश (अर्जुन) के इस प्रकार कहने पर हृषीकेश (श्रीकृष्ण) ने उस उत्तम रथ को दोनों सेनाओं के बीच में खड़ा कर दिया।
verses.english_meaning: Sanjaya said: O Bharata (Dhritarashtra), having been addressed in this way by Arjuna (Gudakesha), Krishna (Hrishikesha) placed the magnificent chariot between the two armies.
verses.context:
Arjuna has asked Krishna to position their chariot between the two armies.

Krishna does exactly that.

Notice something: Krishna doesn't argue with Arjuna's request or rush him into battle. He simply takes him to the place from where he can see the situation clearly.

What Arjuna sees next will change his state of mind completely.
verses.life_lesson:
Sometimes, the best thing someone can do for us isn't to give us advice or make decisions on our behalf.

It's to help us face the situation clearly, even when the truth might be uncomfortable.

There are moments when we don't need someone to solve our problems; we need someone who helps us see them properly.
verses.spiritual_meaning:
Krishna is often understood here as the guide or higher consciousness, while Arjuna represents the human mind seeking direction.

The deeper lesson is that wisdom doesn't always remove difficult situations. Sometimes, it helps us look at them with clarity.
verses.reflection_question: When you're facing something difficult, do you prefer someone to give you a direct solution, or someone who helps you understand the situation so you can reach your own decision?

verses.index_title: Behold the Kurus
verses.index_summary: Facing Bhishma, Drona and the kings, Krishna tells Arjuna to look at the assembled Kurus.
verses.sanskrit_text:
भीष्मद्रोणप्रमुखतः सर्वेषां च महीक्षिताम्।
उवाच पार्थ पश्यैतान्समवेतान्कुरूनिति॥ १.२५॥
verses.transliteration:
Bhīṣma-Droṇa-pramukhataḥ sarveṣāṁ ca mahīkṣitām,
Uvāca Pārtha paśyaitān samavetān Kurūn iti.
verses.hindi_meaning: भीष्म, द्रोण और सभी राजाओं के सामने (रथ खड़ा करके श्रीकृष्ण ने) कहा: हे पार्थ (अर्जुन)! यहाँ एकत्र हुए इन कुरुवंशियों को देखो।
verses.english_meaning: In the presence of Bhishma, Drona, and all the other kings, Krishna said: O Partha (Arjuna), look at all these Kurus gathered here.
verses.context:
Krishna positions the chariot where Arjuna can see the opposing army clearly.

He places it in front of Bhishma and Drona—two people Arjuna deeply respects.

Then Krishna tells him to look at everyone gathered there.

Notice Krishna's choice of words: he calls them the Kurus, reminding Arjuna that these aren't simply enemies; they are members of his own family and community.
verses.life_lesson:
The way we look at a situation can influence how we respond to it.

Calling someone an enemy makes it easier to oppose them. Recognising their relationship with us can make the same decision emotionally difficult.

Sometimes, changing our perspective doesn't change the situation, but it changes how we experience it.
verses.spiritual_meaning:
Krishna is bringing Arjuna face-to-face with reality rather than allowing him to remain focused on an abstract idea of war.

Spiritually, this can represent the importance of awareness: before making a decision, we must be willing to see the complete truth, including the parts we'd rather avoid.
verses.reflection_question: Have you ever found it difficult to stand against someone, correct them, or disagree with them because you respect them or share a close relationship with them—even when you knew they were wrong?

verses.index_title: Arjuna Sees His Own Family
verses.index_summary: Arjuna sees elders, grandfathers, teachers, uncles, brothers, sons, grandsons and friends.
verses.sanskrit_text:
तत्रापश्यत्स्थितान्पार्थः पितॄनथ पितामहान्।
आचार्यान्मातुलान्भ्रातॄन्पुत्रान्पौत्रान्सखींस्तथा॥ १.२६॥
verses.transliteration:
Tatrāpaśyat sthitān Pārthaḥ pitṝn atha pitāmahān,
Ācāryān mātulān bhrātṝn putrān pautrān sakhīṁs tathā.
verses.hindi_meaning: वहाँ पार्थ (अर्जुन) ने (दोनों सेनाओं में) खड़े पिता-तुल्य बड़ों (ताऊ-चाचाओं), पितामहों, आचार्यों, मामाओं, भाइयों, पुत्रों, पौत्रों और मित्रों को देखा।
verses.hindi_meaning_note: *Pitṝn* literally means "fathers". Here it is generally understood to mean the elders of the father's generation, such as paternal uncles, which is how the Hindi meaning renders it.
verses.english_meaning: There, Arjuna saw fathers, grandfathers, teachers, maternal uncles, brothers, sons, grandsons, and friends standing in both armies.
verses.context:
This is where the emotional turning point begins.

Until now, Arjuna has been looking at two opposing armies. But when he actually observes the people standing there, he recognises familiar faces.

These aren't just warriors anymore. They are his relatives, teachers, elders, and friends.

The battlefield that previously represented a duty now becomes a deeply personal conflict.
verses.life_lesson:
Sometimes, a situation looks straightforward until you understand the people involved.

It's easy to make decisions when we look at things from a distance. But when those decisions affect people we love, the same choices can become incredibly difficult.

This is why understanding the emotional consequences of a decision is just as important as understanding its practical consequences.
verses.spiritual_meaning:
Arjuna's vision shifts from seeing opponents to seeing relationships.

This reflects a human struggle: our attachment to people can sometimes make it difficult to distinguish between what we emotionally want and what we believe is right.

The Gita will explore this conflict in much greater depth.
verses.reflection_question: Have you ever found yourself in a situation where your responsibilities or principles required one thing, but your emotional attachment to someone made you want to do the opposite?

verses.index_title: Relatives on Both Sides
verses.index_summary: Arjuna sees fathers-in-law, well-wishers and all his relatives standing in both armies.
verses.sanskrit_text:
श्वशुरान्सुहृदश्चैव सेनयोरुभयोरपि।
तान्समीक्ष्य स कौन्तेयः सर्वान्बन्धूनवस्थितान्॥ १.२७॥
verses.transliteration:
Śvaśurān suhṛdaś caiva senayor ubhayor api,
Tān samīkṣya sa Kaunteyaḥ sarvān bandhūn avasthitān.
verses.hindi_meaning: कुन्तीपुत्र अर्जुन ने दोनों सेनाओं में अपने ससुरों और सुहृदों को भी खड़ा देखा। वहाँ उपस्थित उन सभी बन्धु-बान्धवों को भली-भाँति देखकर…
verses.english_meaning: Arjuna, the son of Kunti, saw his fathers-in-law, well-wishers, and all his relatives standing in both armies.
verses.context:
Arjuna continues recognising familiar people on the battlefield.

He sees not only his immediate family but also people connected to him through marriage and friendship.

The more he observes, the more personal the conflict becomes.

Notice the progression: first he sees two armies, then warriors, and now he sees people with whom he shares relationships.
verses.life_lesson:
Our relationships can influence how we perceive difficult situations.

Someone who appears to be just another person in a crowd may become incredibly important once we understand their connection to us.

It reminds us not to treat people as mere roles or labels. Everyone has a life and relationships of their own.
verses.spiritual_meaning:
Arjuna's growing attachment represents how the mind becomes entangled in relationships and personal connections.

The Gita isn't saying that relationships or affection are wrong. Rather, it will explore how attachment can sometimes cloud our understanding of duty and truth.
verses.reflection_question: Do you find it easier to make decisions when they affect only you, compared to situations where your decisions might affect people you care about?

verses.index_title: Overcome by Compassion
verses.index_summary: Filled with deep compassion and sorrow, Arjuna begins to speak to Krishna.
verses.sanskrit_text:
कृपया परयाविष्टो विषीदन्निदमब्रवीत्।
अर्जुन उवाच।
दृष्ट्वेमं स्वजनं कृष्ण युयुत्सुं समुपस्थितम्॥
verses.transliteration:
Kṛpayā parayāviṣṭo viṣīdann idam abravīt.
Arjuna uvāca:
Dṛṣṭvemaṁ svajanaṁ Kṛṣṇa yuyutsuṁ samupasthitam.
verses.hindi_meaning: (तब) अत्यंत करुणा से भरकर और शोक करते हुए वे यह बोले। अर्जुन ने कहा: हे कृष्ण! युद्ध की इच्छा से सामने खड़े अपने इन स्वजनों को देखकर…
verses.english_meaning: Overcome by deep compassion and sorrow, Arjuna said: O Krishna, seeing my own people gathered here, eager to fight...
verses.context:
This is where Arjuna's emotional struggle becomes visible.

After recognising his relatives, teachers, and friends, he is overwhelmed by compassion and sorrow.

Until now, he was prepared to fight. But seeing his own people standing before him has shaken his resolve.

Notice that Arjuna hasn't yet decided to abandon the battle. He's beginning to express the emotional conflict within him.
verses.life_lesson:
Even people who appear confident and prepared can experience emotional vulnerability when reality finally confronts them.

Feeling conflicted doesn't automatically mean you're weak. It means something matters deeply to you.

However, it's important not to let a strong emotion become the only basis for a major decision.
verses.spiritual_meaning:
Arjuna's compassion is genuine, but it is mixed with attachment and sorrow.

The Gita begins exploring an important distinction: compassion is valuable, but when attachment clouds our judgement, even a good emotion can make it difficult to recognise our responsibility.
verses.reflection_question: When you feel emotionally overwhelmed, do you prefer keeping those feelings to yourself until you understand them, or do you express them to someone you trust?

verses.index_title: Arjuna's Body Gives Way
verses.index_summary: Arjuna trembles, his hair stands on end, his bow Gandiva slips and his skin burns.
verses.sanskrit_text:
वेपथुश्च शरीरे मे रोमहर्षश्च जायते।
गाण्डीवं स्रंसते हस्तात्त्वक्चैव परिदह्यते॥ १.२९॥
verses.transliteration:
Vepathuś ca śarīre me roma-harṣaś ca jāyate,
Gāṇḍīvaṁ sraṁsate hastāt tvak caiva paridahyate.
verses.hindi_meaning: मेरे शरीर में कम्पन हो रहा है और रोंगटे खड़े हो रहे हैं। गाण्डीव धनुष मेरे हाथ से फिसल रहा है और मेरी त्वचा भी जल रही है।
verses.english_meaning: My body is trembling, my hair is standing on end, my bow Gandiva is slipping from my hand, and my skin is burning.
verses.context:
Arjuna's emotional distress is now affecting him physically.

In the previous verse, he expressed his sorrow after seeing his relatives. Now we see how intensely that emotion is affecting his body.

His confidence and readiness to fight are beginning to collapse.
verses.life_lesson:
Emotions aren't merely thoughts in our minds. They can affect our bodies, decisions, behaviour, and ability to function.

Sometimes, we don't realise how overwhelmed we are until our body starts showing it.

Recognising these signs early can help us respond before emotions take control of our actions.
verses.spiritual_meaning:
Arjuna's physical reactions represent the depth of his inner conflict.

Even a capable and accomplished person can become overwhelmed when faced with a situation that challenges their emotional attachments and understanding of duty.

The Gita reminds us that inner stability is something we must cultivate, especially during difficult circumstances.
verses.reflection_question: When you're under extreme emotional pressure, have you noticed physical signs such as trembling, a racing heartbeat, headaches, or difficulty thinking clearly?

verses.index_title: A Mind That Cannot Stay Steady
verses.index_summary: Arjuna cannot hold himself steady; his mind reels and he sees only bad omens.
verses.sanskrit_text:
न च शक्नोम्यवस्थातुं भ्रमतीव च मे मनः।
निमित्तानि च पश्यामि विपरीतानि केशव॥ १.३०॥
verses.transliteration:
Na ca śaknomy avasthātuṁ bhramatīva ca me manaḥ,
Nimittāni ca paśyāmi viparītāni Keśava.
verses.hindi_meaning: मैं (स्थिर) खड़ा रहने में भी समर्थ नहीं हूँ और मेरा मन मानो चक्कर खा रहा है। हे केशव (श्रीकृष्ण)! मुझे लक्षण भी विपरीत (अशुभ) ही दिखाई दे रहे हैं।
verses.english_meaning: I am unable to remain steady. My mind seems to be spinning, and I see only negative or unfavourable signs, O Keshava (Krishna).
verses.context:
Arjuna's distress has deepened.

His body is trembling, his bow is slipping, and now he says that he cannot even keep himself steady. His mind is overwhelmed, and he has begun interpreting everything as a bad sign.

Notice the progression: first he sees his relatives, then feels sorrow, then experiences physical symptoms, and now his thinking itself is becoming clouded.
verses.life_lesson:
When we're emotionally overwhelmed, our minds can start imagining the worst possible outcomes.

A situation that might have several possible endings can suddenly feel as though only one negative ending is possible.

This is why it's important not to make major decisions solely based on what we feel during our most emotionally intense moments.
verses.spiritual_meaning:
Arjuna's mind has lost its steadiness. In spiritual terms, this reflects how attachment and emotional disturbance can cloud our ability to see reality clearly.

The Gita will gradually explore how to develop a mind that remains balanced even when circumstances are difficult.
verses.reflection_question: When something goes wrong, do you tend to imagine multiple possible outcomes, including the worst ones, or are you generally able to keep your mind focused on what you can actually control?

verses.index_title: No Good in Killing One's Own
verses.index_summary: Arjuna sees bad omens and no good in killing his own relatives in battle.
verses.sanskrit_text:
निमित्तानि च पश्यामि विपरीतानि केशव।
न च श्रेयोऽनुपश्यामि हत्वा स्वजनमाहवे॥ १.३१॥
verses.transliteration:
Nimittāni ca paśyāmi viparītāni Keśava,
Na ca śreyo 'nupaśyāmi hatvā svajanam āhave.
verses.hindi_meaning: हे केशव (श्रीकृष्ण)! मुझे लक्षण भी विपरीत (अशुभ) ही दिखाई दे रहे हैं, और युद्ध में अपने ही स्वजनों को मारकर मुझे कोई कल्याण भी दिखाई नहीं देता।
verses.english_meaning: O Keshava (Krishna), I see unfavourable signs, and I cannot see any good coming from killing my own relatives in this battle.
verses.context:
Arjuna is now questioning the purpose of the war itself.

Earlier, he was prepared to fight because he believed it was his duty. But after seeing his relatives and loved ones on the opposing side, he can no longer see any meaningful outcome in victory.

His perspective has shifted from winning the battle to questioning what winning would actually cost.
verses.life_lesson:
Sometimes, achieving something isn't the same as gaining something meaningful.

Before pursuing a goal, it's worth asking yourself:

What am I trying to achieve?

What might I have to sacrifice?

Will the outcome still be worthwhile after those sacrifices?

Not every victory is worth its price.
verses.spiritual_meaning:
Arjuna is struggling to distinguish between external success and true well-being.

The Gita begins questioning the idea that simply achieving what we desire necessarily leads to happiness or righteousness.
verses.reflection_question: Have you ever wanted something very badly, but when you understood what you might have to sacrifice to achieve it, you started questioning whether it was worth pursuing?

verses.index_title: No Desire for Victory or Kingdom
verses.index_summary: Arjuna wants neither victory, kingdom nor pleasures, and asks what use they would be.
verses.sanskrit_text:
न काङ्क्षे विजयं कृष्ण न च राज्यं सुखानि च।
किं नो राज्येन गोविन्द किं भोगैर्जीवितेन वा॥ १.३२॥
verses.transliteration:
Na kāṅkṣe vijayaṁ Kṛṣṇa na ca rājyaṁ sukhāni ca,
Kiṁ no rājyena Govinda kiṁ bhogair jīvitena vā.
verses.hindi_meaning: हे कृष्ण! मैं न विजय चाहता हूँ, न राज्य और न ही सुख। हे गोविन्द (श्रीकृष्ण)! हमें ऐसे राज्य से, भोगों से अथवा जीवन से भी क्या प्रयोजन है?
verses.english_meaning: O Krishna, I desire neither victory, nor kingdom, nor pleasures. What is the use of a kingdom, enjoyment, or even life itself?
verses.context:
Arjuna's emotional conflict has reached another level.

Earlier, he questioned whether killing his relatives was worthwhile. Now he questions the very things he was supposed to fight for: victory, kingdom, and enjoyment.

His reasoning is that these achievements would mean little if the people with whom he wanted to share them were no longer there.
verses.life_lesson:
Achievements often become meaningful because of the people we share them with.

A promotion, success, wealth, or recognition may feel incomplete when the people who matter to us aren't part of our happiness.

But there's another side to this: don't make your entire sense of purpose dependent on another person's presence. Your life and aspirations still have value independently.
verses.spiritual_meaning:
Arjuna is beginning to question worldly achievements and pleasures.

The Gita uses this moment to open a deeper discussion about the difference between temporary happiness and lasting fulfilment.
verses.reflection_question: When you imagine your future success, do you picture yourself enjoying it independently, or do you naturally imagine certain people standing beside you and sharing those moments?

verses.index_title: Those for Whom We Want the Kingdom
verses.index_summary: The people for whose sake kingdom and pleasures are desired stand ready to give up their lives.
verses.sanskrit_text:
येषामर्थे काङ्क्षितं नो राज्यं भोगाः सुखानि च।
त इमेऽवस्थिता युद्धे प्राणांस्त्यक्त्वा धनानि च॥ १.३३॥
verses.transliteration:
Yeṣām arthe kāṅkṣitaṁ no rājyaṁ bhogāḥ sukhāni ca,
Ta ime 'vasthitā yuddhe prāṇāṁs tyaktvā dhanāni ca.
verses.hindi_meaning: जिनके लिए हम राज्य, भोग और सुख चाहते हैं, वे ही लोग अपने प्राणों और धन का मोह त्यागकर इस युद्ध में खड़े हैं।
verses.english_meaning: Those for whose sake we desire kingdom, enjoyment, and happiness are standing here on the battlefield, ready to sacrifice their lives and wealth.
verses.context:
Arjuna explains why victory has lost its meaning for him.

The people with whom he wanted to share his success are now standing against him, prepared to fight and possibly die.

Think about the connection with the previous verse: he doesn't want victory without his people, and now he is looking directly at those very people.
verses.life_lesson:
Sometimes, we pursue goals for the people we love, hoping that one day we can share the rewards with them.

But don't forget that relationships and achievements both need attention. Don't become so occupied with building a future for your loved ones that you forget to value the present you have with them.
verses.spiritual_meaning:
Arjuna's attachment to his loved ones is becoming the centre of his reasoning.

The Gita is gradually revealing how even genuine love and affection can create inner conflict when they become entangled with our sense of duty.
verses.reflection_question: Have you ever postponed your own happiness or personal goals because you wanted someone important to you to be happy first?

verses.index_title: Teachers, Elders and Kinsmen
verses.index_summary: Arjuna names the teachers, elders and relatives standing on the battlefield.
verses.sanskrit_text:
आचार्याः पितरः पुत्रास्तथैव च पितामहाः।
मातुलाः श्वशुराः पौत्राः श्यालाः सम्बन्धिनस्तथा॥ १.३४॥
verses.transliteration:
Ācāryāḥ pitaraḥ putrās tathaiva ca pitāmahāḥ,
Mātulāḥ śvaśurāḥ pautrāḥ śyālāḥ sambandhinas tathā.
verses.hindi_meaning: आचार्य, पिता-तुल्य बड़े, पुत्र, पितामह, मामा, ससुर, पौत्र, साले और अन्य संबंधी भी (यहाँ खड़े हैं)।
verses.english_meaning: Teachers, fathers, sons, grandfathers, maternal uncles, fathers-in-law, grandsons, brothers-in-law, and other relatives are all standing here.
verses.context:
Arjuna continues identifying the people standing on the battlefield.

Notice how specifically he lists his relationships. He isn't looking at an anonymous army anymore. He is seeing individual people who have played different roles in his life.

The emotional weight of the situation is becoming harder for him to bear.
verses.life_lesson:
People occupy different places in our lives. Some guide us, some protect us, some depend on us, and some grow alongside us.

When we face difficult decisions involving these people, we may feel pulled in several directions.

But remember: loving someone doesn't mean agreeing with everything they do, and respecting someone doesn't mean abandoning your own principles.
verses.spiritual_meaning:
This verse illustrates how deeply human relationships can influence our judgement.

The Gita is preparing us to examine the difference between genuine compassion, emotional attachment, and our responsibilities.
verses.reflection_question: Do you find yourself behaving differently around different people depending on how important they are in your life? For example, are you more patient, protective, or forgiving with the people closest to you?

verses.index_title: Not Even for the Three Worlds
verses.index_summary: Arjuna would not kill them even if they attacked him, not even for rule over the three worlds.
verses.sanskrit_text:
एतान्न हन्तुमिच्छामि घ्नतोऽपि मधुसूदन।
अपि त्रैलोक्यराज्यस्य हेतोः किं नु महीकृते॥ १.३५॥
verses.transliteration:
Etān na hantum icchāmi ghnato 'pi Madhusūdana,
Api trailokya-rājyasya hetoḥ kiṁ nu mahī-kṛte.
verses.hindi_meaning: हे मधुसूदन (श्रीकृष्ण)! ये लोग मुझे मार भी डालें, तब भी मैं इन्हें मारना नहीं चाहता — तीनों लोकों के राज्य के लिए भी नहीं, फिर इस पृथ्वी के लिए तो कहना ही क्या?
verses.english_meaning: O Madhusudana (Krishna), I do not wish to kill these people, even if they attack me. Not even for the sovereignty of all three worlds, let alone for an earthly kingdom.
verses.context:
Arjuna's reluctance has now become explicit.

He says that he doesn't want to fight these people even if they attack him. He considers no kingdom or worldly reward valuable enough to justify killing them.

Notice how far he has moved from his initial determination to fight.
verses.life_lesson:
Not everything should be measured by what we stand to gain.

Sometimes, personal values and relationships matter more than rewards, recognition, or material success.

However, there's an important distinction: refusing to harm someone out of compassion is different from allowing someone to harm you or others without standing up against it.
verses.spiritual_meaning:
Arjuna's compassion is real, but his judgement is becoming clouded by attachment.

This is an important tension in the Gita: how do we remain compassionate without abandoning our responsibilities?

Krishna's teachings will gradually address this.
verses.reflection_question: If someone you deeply care about repeatedly hurts you or behaves wrongly, would you eventually stand against them, or would your attachment make it difficult to take a firm position?

verses.index_title: What Joy in Killing the Kauravas?
verses.index_summary: Arjuna asks what happiness could come from killing even aggressors, fearing that only sin would follow.
verses.sanskrit_text:
निहत्य धार्तराष्ट्रान्नः का प्रीतिः स्याज्जनार्दन।
पापमेवाश्रयेदस्मान्हत्वैतानाततायिनः॥ १.३६॥
verses.transliteration:
Nihatya dhārtarāṣṭrān naḥ kā prītiḥ syāj Janārdana,
Pāpam evāśrayed asmān hatvaitān ātatāyinaḥ.
verses.hindi_meaning: हे जनार्दन! धृतराष्ट्र के पुत्रों को मारकर हमें क्या प्रसन्नता मिलेगी? इन आततायियों (आक्रमण करने वालों) को मारने से तो पाप ही हमारे ऊपर आएगा।
verses.english_meaning: O Janardana, what happiness could we possibly gain by killing the sons of Dhritarashtra? Even though they are aggressors, killing them would only bring sin upon us.
verses.context:
Arjuna is continuing to explain why he does not want to fight.

Notice something important: in this verse, Arjuna himself acknowledges that the Kauravas are *ātatāyinaḥ* — aggressors who have committed serious wrongs.

He isn't unaware of their wrongdoing. He knows they have acted unjustly.

Yet he asks Krishna: even if they are aggressors, what happiness could possibly come from killing them?

For Arjuna, this is no longer simply a question of winning or losing a war. He is questioning the moral consequences of his actions.

He fears that even if they win the battle, the victory may come at the cost of their own righteousness.
verses.life_lesson:
Sometimes, doing what is necessary doesn't necessarily feel good.

There are situations where you may have to confront someone, hold them accountable, or protect yourself or others—even when you don't want to hurt that person.

But there's an important distinction between doing something because it is right and doing something because you want revenge.

Before taking an important action, it's worth asking yourself:

*Even if I achieve what I want, will I be at peace with the way I achieved it?*
verses.spiritual_meaning:
Arjuna is struggling with the difference between *Dharma* (righteous duty) and *Pāpa* (sinful action).

He believes that killing his relatives, even when they have committed serious wrongs, may bring spiritual consequences.

However, remember that this is Arjuna's perspective during his moment of confusion. Krishna's teachings will gradually help him understand that Dharma cannot always be judged by emotions alone. One must also consider intention, responsibility, and righteousness.
verses.reflection_question: Have you ever found yourself avoiding confrontation with someone—not because you believed they were right, but because you didn't want to become the reason they felt hurt?

verses.index_title: How Could We Be Happy?
verses.index_summary: Arjuna concludes that killing their own kinsmen could never bring them happiness.
verses.sanskrit_text:
तस्मान्नार्हा वयं हन्तुं धार्तराष्ट्रान्स्वबान्धवान्।
स्वजनं हि कथं हत्वा सुखिनः स्याम माधव॥ १.३७॥
verses.transliteration:
Tasmān nārhā vayaṁ hantuṁ dhārtarāṣṭrān svabāndhavān,
Svajanaṁ hi kathaṁ hatvā sukhinaḥ syāma Mādhava.
verses.hindi_meaning: इसलिए हे माधव (श्रीकृष्ण)! अपने ही संबंधियों और स्वजनों, अर्थात् धृतराष्ट्र के पुत्रों को मारना हमारे लिए उचित नहीं है। अपने ही लोगों को मारकर हम सुखी कैसे हो सकते हैं?
verses.english_meaning: Therefore, O Madhava (a name of Lord Krishna), we should not kill the sons of Dhritarashtra, who are our own relatives. How could we ever be happy after killing our own kinsmen?
verses.context:
Arjuna is taking his argument a step further.

In the previous verse, he questioned what happiness they could gain from killing the Kauravas. Now he reaches a conclusion: killing their own relatives cannot possibly lead to happiness.

Notice how Arjuna keeps returning to the idea of *Svajana* — one's own people.

For him, these aren't simply opponents on a battlefield. They are people with whom he has shared family ties, memories, and relationships.

His emotional attachment is becoming stronger than his sense of duty, and he is struggling to imagine a future in which victory could bring him happiness.
verses.life_lesson:
Sometimes, the hardest decisions are not between right and wrong, but between two things that matter to us.

You might know what needs to be done, but the people involved make the decision emotionally difficult.

This is especially true when relationships are involved. We may tolerate things, delay decisions, or question ourselves because we don't want to lose someone important.

But one thing worth remembering is that being someone’s own person doesn't automatically make their actions right, just as standing against them doesn't automatically make you wrong.
verses.spiritual_meaning:
Arjuna is identifying himself strongly through his relationships.

His thinking is centred on *my family, my relatives, my people*. This attachment (*Moha*) is clouding his ability to look at the situation objectively.

The Gita does not teach us to stop loving people. Rather, it teaches us not to let attachment prevent us from recognising our responsibilities.

Love and compassion are important, but they must exist alongside wisdom and Dharma.
verses.reflection_question: When someone you love makes a decision that you strongly disagree with, do you find yourself questioning your own judgement because you don't want to disappoint or lose that person?

verses.index_title: Blinded by Greed
verses.index_summary: Arjuna says the Kauravas, overcome by greed, cannot see the wrong of destroying a family.
verses.sanskrit_text:
यद्यप्येते न पश्यन्ति लोभोपहतचेतसः।
कुलक्षयकृतं दोषं मित्रद्रोहे च पातकम्॥ १.३८॥
verses.transliteration:
Yady apy ete na paśyanti lobhopahata-cetasaḥ,
Kula-kṣaya-kṛtaṁ doṣaṁ mitra-drohe ca pātakam.
verses.hindi_meaning: यद्यपि लोभ से जिनकी बुद्धि भ्रष्ट हो चुकी है, वे लोग परिवार के नाश से उत्पन्न होने वाले दोष और मित्रों के साथ विश्वासघात करने के पाप को नहीं देख पा रहे हैं।
verses.english_meaning: Even though these people, whose minds have been overcome by greed, fail to recognise the wrongfulness of destroying a family and the sin involved in betraying one's own friends and relatives...
verses.context:
Arjuna is now making an important distinction between himself and the Kauravas.

He believes that the Kauravas are so consumed by greed that they cannot recognise the consequences of their actions.

According to him, their desire for power and kingdom has blinded them to the destruction of their own family and the betrayal of their relationships.

Notice something interesting: Arjuna is not saying that the Kauravas are unaware of the conflict. He is arguing that their greed has made them unable to recognise its deeper moral consequences.

This verse is also connected to the next one, where Arjuna explains why he believes that he and the Pandavas should avoid committing the same wrongdoing.
verses.life_lesson:
Sometimes people become so focused on what they want that they stop considering what their actions might cost others.

Greed, anger, ambition, and even personal ego can make someone overlook relationships and responsibilities.

But there's another lesson hidden here:

Someone else's inability to recognise their mistake doesn't give us permission to stop recognising our own responsibilities.

You cannot always control whether someone understands their mistake, but you can control whether you allow their actions to determine your own values.
verses.spiritual_meaning:
The key word in this verse is *Lobha* (greed).

In Hindu philosophy, greed is one of the inner enemies that disturb a person's judgement. When greed dominates the mind, a person begins prioritising personal desires over Dharma.

Arjuna recognises this problem in the Kauravas, but his own judgement is also clouded by emotional attachment and grief.

This creates an interesting contrast: he can see the attachment and greed influencing others, but he is still struggling to recognise how his own emotions are influencing him.
verses.reflection_question: Have you ever been so focused on protecting a relationship or keeping someone happy that you overlooked something you knew wasn't right?

verses.index_title: Why Not Turn Away from This Wrong?
verses.index_summary: Arjuna asks why they, who see the harm of destroying a family, should not step back.
verses.sanskrit_text:
कथं न ज्ञेयमस्माभिः पापादस्मान्निवर्तितुम्।
कुलक्षयकृतं दोषं प्रपश्यद्भिर्जनार्दन॥ १.३९॥
verses.transliteration:
Kathaṁ na jñeyam asmābhiḥ pāpād asmān nivartitum,
Kula-kṣaya-kṛtaṁ doṣaṁ prapaśyadbhir Janārdana.
verses.hindi_meaning: हे जनार्दन (श्रीकृष्ण)! जब हम परिवार के विनाश से उत्पन्न होने वाले दोष को स्पष्ट रूप से देख रहे हैं, तो फिर हमें इस पाप से पीछे हटने का विचार क्यों नहीं करना चाहिए?
verses.english_meaning: O Janardana (Lord Krishna), since we clearly understand the evils that arise from the destruction of a family, should we not refrain from committing this sinful act?
verses.context:
Arjuna is now questioning why the Pandavas should proceed with the war when they can already recognise its possible consequences.

His argument is essentially:

"If the Kauravas are blinded by greed and cannot understand the consequences of their actions, we can understand them. So why should we commit the same wrongdoing when we know better?"

Notice the shift in his reasoning.

Earlier, Arjuna spoke about his attachment to relatives and friends. Now he is appealing to awareness and responsibility.

He believes that knowing something is wrong should be enough reason to step away from it.
verses.life_lesson:
There's a difference between knowing what is right and actually having the courage to act accordingly.

Sometimes we recognise that a situation is harmful, that a decision is wrong, or that a relationship is becoming unhealthy. Yet we continue because stepping away is emotionally difficult.

But awareness comes with responsibility.

If you recognise a mistake, you also have to ask yourself what you're going to do with that knowledge.
verses.spiritual_meaning:
This verse highlights *Viveka* — the ability to distinguish between right and wrong, beneficial and harmful, temporary desires and lasting values.

Arjuna believes that because he can recognise the consequences of the war, he has a responsibility to avoid participating in it.

However, the larger teaching of the Gita will explore an important distinction: recognising that an action has consequences is not always the same as correctly understanding one's Dharma.

Sometimes, even avoiding action can have consequences.
verses.reflection_question: Have you ever known what you should do in a situation, but still struggled to do it because emotionally, it was much harder than simply knowing the right thing?

verses.index_title: When a Family Is Destroyed
verses.index_summary: Arjuna fears that family traditions perish, and unrighteousness spreads, when a family is destroyed.
verses.sanskrit_text:
कुलक्षये प्रणश्यन्ति कुलधर्माः सनातनाः।
धर्मे नष्टे कुलं कृत्स्नमधर्मोऽभिभवत्युत॥ १.४०॥
verses.transliteration:
Kula-kṣaye praṇaśyanti kula-dharmāḥ sanātanāḥ,
Dharme naṣṭe kulaṁ kṛtsnam adharmo 'bhibhavaty uta.
verses.hindi_meaning: परिवार के नष्ट हो जाने पर उसके प्राचीन और परंपरागत पारिवारिक धर्म (रीति-रिवाज, मूल्य और कर्तव्य) नष्ट हो जाते हैं। जब धर्म का नाश होता है, तब पूरे परिवार में अधर्म का प्रभाव बढ़ने लगता है।
verses.english_meaning: When a family is destroyed, its long-established traditions and values also perish. When righteousness and those guiding principles are lost, unrighteousness begins to prevail throughout the entire family.
verses.context:
Arjuna now explains why he believes the destruction of a family is so serious.

He isn't thinking only about the people who will die in the war. He is thinking about the generations that will come after them.

In his understanding, a family carries more than blood relationships. It also carries traditions, values, responsibilities, and ways of living that are passed from one generation to another.

He fears that when the people who preserve and teach these values are lost, the entire family structure may gradually collapse.

This is why Arjuna sees the consequences of war as extending far beyond the battlefield.
verses.life_lesson:
A family or community is not held together by relationships alone. It is also held together by shared values, mutual respect, and the lessons passed from one generation to another.

Think about it: children often learn how to treat others, handle responsibilities, respect people, and make decisions by observing the people around them.

When those values disappear, the impact can extend much further than the people directly involved.

What we pass on to the next generation can sometimes matter more than what we leave behind materially.
verses.spiritual_meaning:
The central concept here is *Kula-Dharma* — the duties, values, and traditions that sustain a family.

Arjuna believes that preserving these values is essential for maintaining harmony and righteousness within society.

The verse also introduces the relationship between *Dharma* and *Adharma*: when righteous principles are neglected, unrighteous behaviour can gain influence.

However, we should remember that Arjuna is presenting his understanding of the consequences of war. Krishna's response will later help examine Dharma from a broader perspective.
verses.reflection_question: Do you believe that the values and behaviour of a family are shaped more by what parents and elders teach directly, or by what younger generations observe them doing in everyday life? Why?

verses.index_title: The Consequences of Adharma and Social Disorder
verses.index_summary: Arjuna fears that when unrighteousness prevails, families are corrupted and social disorder follows.
verses.sanskrit_text:
अधर्माभिभवात्कृष्ण प्रदुष्यन्ति कुलस्त्रियः।
स्त्रीषु दुष्टासु वार्ष्णेय जायते वर्णसङ्करः॥ १.४१॥
verses.transliteration:
Adharmābhibhavāt Kṛṣṇa praduṣyanti kula-striyaḥ,
Strīṣu duṣṭāsu Vārṣṇeya jāyate varṇa-saṅkaraḥ.
verses.hindi_meaning: हे कृष्ण (श्रीकृष्ण)! अधर्म के बढ़ने से परिवार की स्त्रियाँ दूषित हो जाती हैं। हे वार्ष्णेय (वृष्णि वंश में जन्मे श्रीकृष्ण)! स्त्रियों के दूषित होने पर वर्णसंकर उत्पन्न होता है।
verses.hindi_meaning_note: This is a traditional translation of the verse. The terms *kula-striyaḥ* and *varṇa-saṅkara* carry historical and social meanings, and different commentators interpret them differently. We should understand the verse in its ancient context rather than treating its social assumptions as universal truths today.
verses.english_meaning: O Krishna, when unrighteousness prevails, the women of the family become vulnerable to corruption. And when the women are thus corrupted, social disorder and confusion of lineage arise.
verses.context:
Arjuna is continuing his argument about what he believes will happen after the destruction of families.

In the social structure of his time, women were closely associated with maintaining family traditions, customs, and continuity between generations.

Arjuna fears that war will destroy the stability of families, leaving people vulnerable to exploitation and social disorder.

The term *Varṇa-saṅkara* refers to the mixing or confusion of social and familial classifications. It reflects the social concerns and assumptions of the period in which this dialogue is set.

It is important to recognise that Arjuna is expressing his understanding of society at this moment. The verse is not a statement that women are responsible for maintaining the morality of an entire society.
verses.life_lesson:
When a society becomes unstable, its most vulnerable members often suffer first.

Conflict doesn't affect everyone equally. Children, women, the elderly, and people who depend on others can face consequences far beyond the original disagreement.

This verse invites us to think about the people who may suffer indirectly because of decisions made by others.

A responsible decision should consider not only the people directly involved, but also those who have no control over the situation.
verses.spiritual_meaning:
The broader theme is the relationship between *Dharma* and social harmony.

Arjuna fears that when righteousness disappears, the structures that protect people and pass values between generations will also weaken.

The deeper concern is the breakdown of social responsibility and the suffering that follows.

As we continue, we'll see how Krishna challenges Arjuna's reasoning and helps him look beyond fear and attachment.
verses.reflection_question: When a conflict happens between two people, do you naturally think about the people directly involved, or do you also consider how their actions might affect everyone around them—even those who have nothing to do with the conflict?
